citation.title: The extent of algorithm aversion in decision-making situations with varying gravity

reading.source_scope_note: Human choices between labeled higher- and lower-success options implemented through monetary lotteries, not direct tests of deployed algorithms or actual clinical/legal decisions. Earlier cited primary studies were not independently read here.
access_limits: All 21 extracted pages read, including the definition-review table, other result tables, figures’ captions, limitations and references. Table 7 on PDF page 14 was rendered and visually inspected; plots were not independently digitized.
Supporting instructions, comprehension checks, scenario texts and raw XLSX data were linked but not included in this PDF and were not examined.

study.design: Between-subject six-domain framing experiment; one frame per student
study.incentive: €2 show-up and €4 success bonus, identical across domains; visible card lotteries implement stated 70% algorithm versus 60% human success
study.outcome: Binary source choice; prior perceived-gravity rating from 0 to 10

summary: 56 of 143 chose the human-labeled 60%-success option over the algorithm-labeled 70%-success option. Human choice was 49.30% in the serious-domain cluster and 29.17% in the less-serious-domain cluster. The authors report an association between perceived gravity and lower algorithm choice. Actual monetary stakes were fixed; different domains varied together with seriousness, so this does not isolate real stakes or seriousness as a single causal mechanism.

findings.term: Algorithm aversion has heterogeneous definitions and contextual conditions
findings.definition: The literature uses both a broad reluctance-to-use definition and a narrower rejection-of-known-superior-advice definition; the current experiment adopts the latter and finds more rejection in serious-domain frames.
findings.novelty_rationale: This is a third read source and a boundary refinement for the existing concept, not a new behaviour for every domain or the authors’ tragedy-of-aversion phrase.

evidence.quote: defined the term algorithm aversion in quite different ways
variation in gravity between different scenarios

findings.evidence_scope: 143 students chose between stated 70%- and 60%-success lotteries under six service descriptions. The serious-versus-trivial cluster contrast was reported at p=.014; narrower definition and fixed financial outcomes matter to interpretation.
findings.boundary: Distinguish general disapproval, reduced use after errors, and rejection of a demonstrably superior option. A lower financial expected value does not by itself establish violation of every legitimate procedural or ethical value. Seriousness was not manipulated within a single domain, and no real patient, criminal defendant or vehicle user experienced the narrated harm.

findings.term: Narrative frame can alter source choice with fixed monetary probabilities
findings.definition: Choice between fixed-probability human- and algorithm-labeled lotteries varied across service-domain descriptions, illustrating contextual influence beyond the monetary payoff structure.
findings.novelty_rationale: The framing entry already covers context-dependent answers. This adds a human decision experiment rather than another independent AI-output effect.

evidence.quote: many other associations with the decision-making situations

findings.evidence_scope: Between-subject domain frames included driving, MRI interpretation, criminal files, dating, cooking and weather. Perceived gravity was measured; it was not independently randomized or isolated from moral, familiarity or complexity associations.
findings.boundary: Mathematically matched lotteries need not make the narratives identical in every decision-relevant meaning. Do not call this merely a harmless wording perturbation, infer a humanlike framing mechanism inside an AI, or conceal material risks to increase user adoption.

methodological_limits: Small student sample, about 22–25 participants per domain; no professional or population representativeness demonstrated.
The perceived seriousness rating and choice are associated; regression does not remove cross-domain confounds or identify gravity as the sole cause.
High- and low-gravity narratives had identical financial stakes and no real third-party harms. Claims about actual emergency decisions require new evidence.
Table 7 explores ten three-versus-three partitions. Comparing nominal p-values across such partitions does not establish that gravity is uniquely the most important causal factor.

A statement that all participants should choose the algorithm corresponds to a boundary-probability null. The reported goodness-of-fit chi-square statistic is not independently validated here; observed counts should not be mistaken for a verified test against p=1.
The displayed regression aggregates choice percentages by gravity rating; raw-data weighting, model specification and uncertainty were not independently rechecked.
Recipe selection was rated fairly serious (mean 7.87), limiting a sharp interpretation of the trivial label.
The article’s advertising suggestion to avoid pointing out risks was not experimentally tested as a safe intervention and is not adopted as project guidance.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Jauernig concerns discretion and a broad procedure preference. Filiz explicitly adopts a narrower expected-money criterion. Keep both operational definitions visible rather than recast all resistance as irrational.

The significant domain-frame association here and the nonsignificant dismissal/promotion effect in Maasland use different manipulations and outcomes. They support context-specific inquiry, not a universal stakes rule.

deferred.reason: Rhetorical description of aversion in serious-domain frames, not an independently distinct behaviour or a replication across real high-stakes decisions.
Background frameworks used to motivate a prediction that was not supported in its predicted direction. Internal effort and commitment were not directly measured.

limitations: No new standalone behaviour was added. Two existing entries gained source-grounded definitions and conditions.
Three distinct read sources can now be selected for algorithm aversion without substituting the article’s cited-but-unread bibliography.
